props.title: Flash of Genius

sections.content: Flash of Genius stands among the most compelling David-vs-Goliath legal dramas about intellectual property, with Greg Kinnear delivering a powerhouse performance as Robert Kearns, the inventor who took on Ford Motor Company. The film joins other notable inventor biopics like The Current War (2017) and Joy (2015) in exploring the personal toll of innovation and corporate theft. What sets it apart is its laser focus on the intermittent windshield wiper - a seemingly mundane invention that becomes the centerpiece of an epic battle over creative rights and recognition.

sections.content: The film fits into a larger tradition of movies about lone inventors facing massive corporations, like Tucker: The Man and His Dream (1988) and Joy (2015). These stories typically focus on the emotional and financial devastation wreaked upon innovators who refuse to back down. Kinnear's portrayal of Kearns captures both the obsessive dedication required to create and the stubborn determination needed to fight for recognition, echoing similar themes in The Aviator (2004) and The Current War (2017).

What distinguishes Flash of Genius is its commitment to showing the grinding reality of patent litigation without Hollywood glamorization. Unlike Erin Brockovich (2000) or Dark Waters (2019), which inject more dramatic flourishes into their legal battles, this film maintains a deliberately measured pace that mirrors Kearns' years-long struggle. The approach makes his eventual triumph more meaningful and authentic. SUBHEAD: The Human Cost of Innovation

sections.content: The film excels at showing how Kearns' pursuit of justice affects his family, marriage, and mental health. This personal toll echoes through other innovation narratives like The Theory of Everything (2014) and A Beautiful Mind (2001), where genius comes at a steep personal price. Lauren Graham's nuanced performance as Kearns' wife Phyllis adds crucial emotional weight to the story of how obsession can unravel domestic life.
